short: Vacancy-Driven Gelation Using Defect-Rich Nanoassemblies of
title: Vacancy-Driven Gelation Using Defect-Rich Nanoassemblies of 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides and Polymeric Binder for Biomedical Applications

lanes.label: Classical tools
lanes.sub: collapsed to one node per state

states.title: Hypothesis and design
states.head: Cell encapsulation needs a hydrogel that sets without UV or heat, stays stiff and elastic, and tolerates living cells during gelation. Pristine 2D MoS2 has too few planar defects to conjugate polymer chains, and MoS2-driven gelation has not been reported.
states.detail: Absorbed: y1 (HYP/need), y2 (HYP/gap), y3 (HYP/hypothesis), y4 (DES/base_system), y5 (DES/variable_sweep), y6 (PRC/synthesis), y7 (PRC/synthesis). Premises: In 2H MoS2 molybdenum sits in trigonal prismatic coordination bound to six sulfide ligands, so pristine basal planes offer few active centres

states.title: Structure state
states.head: The product is 2H MoS2 at every precursor ratio. The nanosheets assemble into 1-3 um flower-like spheres of rippled, unstacked petals.
states.detail: Absorbed: y8 (STR/phase/identity), y9 (STR/microstructure/shape), y10 (STR/defect/point), y11 (STR/chemistry/bonding). Premises: Ostwald ripening of hydrothermally grown flakes drives their assembly into flower-like structures

states.title: Property state and mechanisms
states.head: The prepolymer turns strongly shear-thinning: consistency K rises from 7.7 to 2479 and the power-law index falls from 1.0 to about 0.17. Compressive modulus rises from 8.7 to 27.7 kPa as MoS2 goes from 0.25 to 2 wt%.

states.title: Performance state
states.head: hMSCs can be encapsulated simply by mixing: the gel sets within 30 min in culture medium and the cells stay viable at 48 h

states.title: Conclusion
states.head: Atomic vacancies in 2D MoS2 act as the crosslinker, giving a stimulus-free, stiff, elastomeric and cell-compatible hydrogel

nodes.title: RAMAN, XRD, F1
nodes.head: The higher-order XRD reflections resolve only at 1:4 and 1:6 while (002) is unchanged, and the rising A1g/E1-2g ratio is itself the standard signature of thicker, more stacked MoS2
nodes.solves: Sulfur-rich feeds leave more atomic vacancies in the lattice, giving more active centres
nodes.note: judge re-read of F1c: the (002) peak has the same width in all four traces - if anything the 1:6 trace is slightly broader at the base - while (103), (006), (105) and (110) go from one unresolved hump at 1:1 to separate peaks at 1:4 and 1:6. So the panel reads as more, not less, crystalline order at the sulfur-rich end. The paper reads the same two observables (this trend and the F1f Raman ratio) as evidence for more defects, while its own text reads the Raman ratio as increased interlayer interaction and crystal thickness; nothing in the packet separates the two.

10.1002/adma.201702037#F1b.definition: SEM image of nanoassemblies shows rippled flakes arranged spherically
use: The hierarchical nanoassemblies were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and showed a typical size of ${\approx}1.5{-}2~{\upmu}\mathrm{m}$ (Figure 1b).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F1d.definition: TEM of the nanoassemblies along with selected area electron diffraction (SAED) confirmed hierarchy of assembled nanostructure
use: These findings suggest the formation of more ordered phase of ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ with increasing thiourea content, which correlates with previous reports.[16,17] The representative transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images along with the SAED pattern indicated the crystalline nature of 2D ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ nanoassemblies (Figure 1d).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F1c.definition: The 2H phase of ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ lattice was confirmed by $\mathsf{X}$ -ray diffraction pattern obtained for different feed precursor ratios (molybdenum:sulfur)
use: The diffraction peaks of nanoassemblies (002, 004, 100, 103, 006, 105 and 110) agree well with the hexagonal ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ (JCPDS card No. 73-1508), indicating the high purity of synthesized ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ (Figure 1c).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F1f.definition: Raman spectra confirmed the presence of two prominent peaks $(\mathsf E^{\rceil}{}_{2\mathrm{g}}$ and $\mathsf{A}_{\mathsf{1g}})$ corresponding to 2H phase, while their intensity ratio supported the consistent increment in intensity related to out-of-plane vibration of S atoms with increase in sulfur feed precursor ratio
use: From the Raman spectra (Figure 1f), in-plane vibrations of two S atoms with respect to Mo $\big(\mathrm{E}^{1}{2\mathrm{g}}\big)$ were blue-shifted from sample 1:1 $(374.3~\mathrm{cm^{-1}})$ to 1:6 $(376.5~\mathrm{cm^{-1}})$ , while the out-of-plane vibration of single S atom, $\mathrm{A_{1g}}$ $(401.8~\mathrm{cm}^{-1})$ remained the same for all samples.
Therefore, we carried out the PL spectra of these nanoassemblies by exciting at $470~\mathrm{nm}$ and recording the emission spectra between 550 and $700\mathrm{nm}$ (Figure 1f).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F1g.definition: Photoluminescence (PL) spectra of ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies depicting the evolution of signals due to defect sites and were directly proportional to the number of active centers

10.1002/adma.201702037#F2d.definition: Gelation kinetics of PEG–SH and $\mathsf{P E G}\mathrm{-}\mathsf{S H}/2\%\mathsf{M o S}_{2}$ confirm vacancy-driven gelation of defect-rich ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies and PEG–SH
use: The gelation kinetics was monitored by placing the prepolymer solution containing four-arm PEG–SH ( $10\%$ , $M_{\mathrm{w}}\approx20~000)$ and ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ nanoassemblies $(2\%)$ in deionized (DI) $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ , and monitoring storage modulus $\left(G^{\prime}\right)$ overtime (Figure 2d).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F4a.definition: Raman spectra of PEG–SH along with gels made with 0.25 and $2\%$ ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ . The thiol vibrations at 670 and $2570^{-1}$ from PEG disappeared in the crosslinked hydrogels due to formation of new bond with ${\sf M o S}_{2}$
use: Raman spectra analysis of PEG–SH shows two thiol peaks at about $670~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ (due to $-\mathrm{SH}$ deformation) and $2570~\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ (due to $-\mathrm{SH}$ stretching) (Figure 4a).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F4b.definition: XPS of hydrogel shows the change in binding energy of carbon (C 1s) peak due to ${\mathsf{C}}{\mathrm{-}}{\mathsf{S}}{\mathrm{-}}{\mathsf{M}}{\mathrm{o}}$ formation while two additional peaks appeared in Mo 3d spectrum belonging to ${\mathsf{P E C}}.{\mathsf{M o S}}_{2}$ . Raman and XPS together suggest the new bond formation at the site of vacancy via chemisorption
use: To corroborate the Raman data on gelation mechanism, we carried out XPS analysis of carbon 1s and molybdenum 3d core level electrons from covalently crosslinked hydrogels and compared them with PEG–SH and ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ (Figure 4b).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F3c.definition: SEM images of a transverse section of hydrogel $(\mathsf{P E G}{\mathrm{-}}\mathsf{S H}/2\%\mathsf{M}$ oS2) show porous and interconnect network. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) spectra and mapping confirmed the presence of Mo and S in the crosslinked network
use: We further carried out scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the transverse section of freeze-dried hydrogels to determine the distribution of ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ nanoassemblies within the crosslinked network (Figure 3c).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F2b.definition: Shear-thinning characteristic of prepolymer solutions. $10\%$ PEG–SH show Newtonian behavior. The viscosity of prepolymer solutions increases with the addition of ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ and display shear-thinning characteristics. Power law model was fitted to determine power law index and consistency coefficient
use: To investigate these interactions, the viscosity of prepolymer solution was determined at different shear rates using a rheometer (Figure 2b).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F3b.definition: Uniaxial compression demonstrates formation of mechanically stiff hydrogel network. The compressive modulus increases from 8 to $25\mathrm{kPa}$ with an increase in ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ concentration from 0.25 to $2\%$
use: The addition of ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ to PEG–SH resulted in linear increase in compressive modulus from $8.6\pm0.6~\mathrm{kPa}$ $(\mathrm{PEG}\mathrm{-SH}/0.25\%\mathrm{MoS}_{2})$ to $27.7\pm1.1~\mathrm{kPa}$ $(\mathrm{PEG}\mathrm{-SH}/2\%\mathrm{MoS}_{2})$ (Figure 3b).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F5b.definition: The viability of cells in presence of different concentrations of ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies was determined using MTT cytotoxicity assay
use: Following these initial assessments, cytotoxicity assay was performed after cells were subjected to increasing concentration of ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ nanoassemblies $(0{-}10\mathrm{mgmL^{-1}};$ (Figure 5b).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F5e.definition: The physical stability of gel in culture media as well as in excess thiol was determined. While the gel maintains its structural integrity in culture media, it gets dissolved in DTT due to presence of excess thiol
use: The stability of nanocomposite hydrogels in cell culture media was monitored for $48\mathrm{~h~}$ to evaluate its ability to support encapsulated cells (Figure 5e). $\mathrm{PEG}{\mathrm{-SH}}/2\%\mathrm{MoS}_{2}$ hydrogels readily swelled (4–6 times) in media and retained the initial shape.

10.1002/adma.201702037#F5f.definition: The facile vacancy-driven gelation between PEG–SH and ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies allows easy cell encapsulation without adversely affecting cell viability $(>85\%)$ after $48~\mathsf{h}$ as observed in the confocal microscopy image (green $=$ live cell, red $=$ dead cell)
use: Cells survive the gelation process and maintain high viability after $^{48\mathrm{~h~}}$ , as evident by high number of live (green) cells compared to dead cells (red) (Figure 5f).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F5d.definition: Gelation kinetics of $\mathsf{P E G}\mathrm{-}\mathsf{S H}$ and $2\%$ ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies (1:4) in culture media exhibited accelerated gelation and stiffer network due to the presence of mineral ions in the media
use: A significant reduction in gelation time and increase in storage modulus $\langle G^{\prime}\approx11\mathrm{kPa}\rangle$ in $1.5\mathrm{~h~}$ was observed (Figure 5d).

10.1002/adma.201702037#F5c.definition: The effect of ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies on cell cycle was evaluated using flow cytometry. The results show that high cell population in $\mathsf{G}2/\mathsf{M}$ phase at lower ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ concentration shifts to apoptosis phase at higher ${\sf M o S}_{2}$ concentrations
use: Despite subjecting cells to $10\mathrm{mgmL^{-1}M o S}_{2}$ nanoassemblies, half maximal inhibitory concentration $(\mathrm{IC}_{50})$ was not observed, while other 2D nanomaterials such as nanosilicates and graphene have $\mathrm{IC}_{50}$ of ${\approx}5{}$ and ${\approx}1~\mathrm{mg}~\mathrm{mL}^{-1}$ , respectively.[19] To investigate the effect of ${\mathrm{MoS}}_{2}$ nanoassemblies on cell proliferation, cell cycle analysis was performed (Figure 5c).
